speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the various items have been adopted with the exception of items 184 and 184a. With respect to that we have made a very careful effort to meet certain criticisms that were urged against it, one of the principal being that the governor in council was perhaps not the best tribunal in the world to make the determinations that were called for under the item as read. It is therefore proposed to make it somewhat clearer than it read. Item 184 would read as follows:
184. Newspapers, unbound, n.o.p.; tailors', milliners' and mantlemakers' fashion plates, when imported in single copies in sheet form with periodical trade journals: magazines published in other than the French or the English language: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
That, hon. members will observe, is substantially item 184 as printed with some slight changes in the wording of the resolution. Then item 184a would read;
184a. Magazines, unbound: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free.
They will thus be free under the British preferential tariff and the intermediate tariff, but not otherwise. Under item 184b these magazines are divided by the application of a new standard of division, as follows:
184b. Magazines, including agricultural, business, technical and trade journals, unbound or paper bound, which, by reason of their advertising content, are subject in the country of origin to zone rates of postage based upon such advertising content:
(i)	w'hen the space devoted to advertisements exceeds 20 per centum, but does not exceed 30 per centum of the total space, per copy: general tariff, 2 cents.
(ii)	when the space devoted to advertisements exceeds 30 per centum of the total space, per copy: general tariff^ 5 cents.
That is the application of two principles:
first, that in the country of origin the magazines are subject to a surtax or higher rate of postage by reason of their advertising content; second, the determination of what per centum of advertising shall subject them to a given standard or rate of duty. The next division is 184c:
184c. Magazines in which the advertising matter does not exceed 20 per centum of the total space: general tariff, free.
Lastly, to meet a difficulty to which I shall presently refer, we would have 184d:
184d. Periodicals or portions of newspapers consisting largely of fiction and/or feature stories or articles and/or, comic supplements, per pound: general tariff, 15 cents.
(The Chairman.]
Provided, that the duty under this tariff item shall be not less than, per copy: general tariff, 15 cents.
Provided, that nothing in tariff items 184, 184a, 184b, 184c or 184d shall affect in any way the provisions of item 1201 of schedule C to the customs tariff.
This is the item in the customs tariff providing for censorship and for the prohibition of magazines and newspapers that fall within the category mentioned.
Provided, further, that the governor in council may make such regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions of tariff items 184, 184a, 184b, 184c and 184d.
Provided, further, that the rates of duty specified in tariff items 184b and 184d shall be effective on and after the first day of September, 1931.
Some question has been raised as to when this should become effective; but inasmuch as magazines with a circulation of 1,000,000 copies or more have to commence printing a month or six weeks before the actual issue, in fairness to such magazines the date of the coming into effect of these items has been made the first day of September next.
May I say to the committee that the matter has not been free from difficulties. For the last twenty-five or thirty years Canada has imposed a tax by way of a tariff upon advertising matter. That tariff amounts to fifteen cents per pound or not less in any event than 35 per cent ad valorem. But amazing as it may sound, that class of advertising that was most potent, namely, the advertising in the magazines, periodicals and newspapers to which I have referred, has been free from the collection of any tariff with respect to advertising. Our great neighbour to the south early learned that it was undesirable to let this condition continue, and so they provided first of all that there should be a tax imposed upon advertising in such periodicals or publications; second, that wherever the amount of advertising exceeded 5 per cent, a graduated rate should apply. That rate was determined by the zone distances that established the rate in parcel post transportation or transmission. These rates are as follows:

As I observed a moment ago, these are the rates charged for parcel post transmission within the United States. It has been found in the United States that the publications which we are seeking to reach by these items average approximately 45 per cent of advertising matter, and the average charge of postage	paid as	a surtax	amounts	to notquite two and one-half cents but 2-45 cents. It will be observed that the rate is slightly higher than the rate we have fixed because we realize the tremendous hold that such publications have upon this country. The circulation is tremendous; as a matter of fact, the ' sum total of the various publications amounts to 1,400,000 copies per issue, as against less than 950,000 of our own. I was recently	reading	a rather	extensive	articleupon the subject and I was somewhat amazed at the extent to which these publications have found a	home in	Canada.Then	there is	another	class altogether.
There is a class which we reach by censorship and a very large number of those publications have been placed under the ban by reason of article 1201 of our tariff, which is the prohibition article to which I referred a moment ago. But there is a class that one would hardly describe as coming within the exact language of the words used in that article, but which is most offensive to a very considerable number of the Canadian people. It was found that the imposition of a high rate of duty would accomplish the end aimed at and in the budget resolution the rate was stated at fifteen cents per pound, which is the rate that will continue.
In the resolution we have endeavoured to be fair, because it is rather late in the day that this action is being taken. It is amazing that we should have continued all these years to tax ordinary advertising and yet permit this form of advertising to remain free from any tariff charge. I have never quite been able to understand just why this is so; I suspect there are many reasons with which I am not familiar, but at any rate, that is the fact. If other countries are right in making this charge on advertising content, I think it cannot be said that we ape treating the matter unfairly by endeavouring to secure some revenue from it ourselves, but we must, as I have said, endeavour to be fair for we have so long continued not to collect any revenue. Therefore, instead of adopting the principle that has been adopted in the United States,
of charging for advertising content beyond 5 per cent, we have left the advertising content up to 20 per cent free from this tariff charge. On advertising content from 20 to 30 per cent we have made the charge, as I have indicated, two cents per copy, but when the space devoted to it exceeds 30 per cent, then the rate is five cents per copy. I read to the committee the rates prevailing by way of surtax in the United States, showing that for transmission of a magazine of the class indicated, where the advertising was in excess of 30 per cent, the rate from the east to San Francisco would be seven cents per copy in addition to the ordinary postage. I think, therefore, it cannot be said that this is in any sense an unfair impost.
Is the tax going to be imposed on a monthly basis, because the quantity of advertising will vary from month to month?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
North Waterloo has asked me- the same question upon which I sought information when I was giving consideration to this matter, and I found that in the United States the publishers are compelled to file with the post office in the community in which the magazine is published a statement of the reading content and the advertising content of each issue as it leaves the press, and that determines the matter so far as they are concerned. In some instances you will find a copy from the press containing 45 or 50 per cent advertising content and 55 or 50 per cent reading content. In this item you will find the words, "which by reason of their advertising content are subject in the country of origin to zone rates of postage based upon such advertising content." That is, magazines which are not published in this country but come in here and have a wide circulation must, in order to fall within the provisions of that item of the tariff, be such as are subject to zone rates by reason of their advertising content. We apply the same principle, with the modification that we have been slightly more generous than in the country of origin for a reason which I think is not difficult to see, and which I think will appeal to the committee. That is, we have no zone system in this country. So in a broad and general way we have sought an average which I think the committee will agree is fairly represented by the charges that are made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The right hon. the Prime Minister has removed so much by way of exception that I find it rather difficult to realize what is left of the original resolution. The resolution as introduced was almost in the nature of an embargo on periodicals and magazines coming from the United States and other countries to this country, and as such it seemed to me to be a tax on thought and literary art. The protest that I wish to make at the moment is against a tax of that character. If the effect of the amendments, which my right hon. friend has just moved, has been to eliminate the greater part of the original resolution, I have little further to say; but as originally introduced, the resolution amounted, as I have said, so far as it concerned magazines and periodicals coming to this country from abroad, to all but a complete embargo, and to that extent to a prohibition upon thought and ideas conveyed through those media to the people of this country.
May I say that thought, as hon. members well know, is cosmopolitan. It should have mo limitation with respect either to place or time. All advances that are made in civilization are the result of ideas, and in any way to preclude the possibility of a good idea having its opportunity of fruition to the full in any quarter is to retard to that extent the progress of civilization itself. In these days there is probably nothing more important than what we now describe as the international mind, that effch nation should begin to appreciate the intellectual ideals and currents of thought that prevail and sway opinion in other countries. Viewed in this light the tax becomes a tax upon international good will. So far as our immediate neighbours are concerned, I venture to say that their thought on the great questions of the day finds its expression in the leading periodicals and publications' of the United States. I believe it is all in the interests of international good will that the people of our country should become as familar as possible with the trends of thought in the United States on all classes of questions, just as it is all important that our neighbours should also become acquainted with our trends of thought and thereby in a more immediate way become familiar with the thought which governs British communities generally. I dleplore any tax which will in any way restrict the widest spread of views and ideas throughout communities, particularly communities that are neighbours.

May I say further that it seems to me a tax of this kind is doing an injustice to our own authors and writers. My right hon. friend has sitting immediately behind him one who has distinguished himself as an author, and only a few days ago in this House of Commons he made the statement that but for the fact that he had been able to place some of his writings in the United States he doubted very much whether they would have found a market at all. If my right hon. friend is going to tax the magazines that come into this country from the United States, I venture to say that it will not be long before American publishers will cease taking contributions from the pens of Canadian authors and poets. Many of our writers have won distinction not only for themselves but for our country through their contributions to some of the large publications in the United States, and an inevitable reaction, it seems to me, to a tax of this kind will be the refusal hereafter by some of these publications of the work of some of the best writers in Canada. In that respect the tax would be a great mistake. How great a mistake no one will ever know, because none of us can value the thing which might have been but which is not because of certain circumstances.
May I mention another fact which comes to my mind, and that is the effect which this tax may have upon tourist travel? That may seem remote, but as we all know the tourist traffic from the United States into Canada is becoming a very important item in the revenues of this oountry. Tourists particularly desire when away from home to receive the publications which they are accustomed to read in their own country, and I do not believe it is stretching the point too far to assume that if our American friends travelling in different parts of Canada find that they can no longer secure at a book store, a hotel or anywhere else, copies of the publications they have been accustomed to read at home, they will prefer in the future a trip to some of their own national parks or * other fields of recreation to coming to Canada. Those are indirect effects, which nevertheless are quite important.
Again, American magazines and periodicals in some part use Canadian newsprint in the preparation of their material for publication, and to the extent to which my right hon. friend's tax operates against some of these magazines coming into Canada, he is dealing

a blow to the pulp and paper industry of this country, on the product of which our neighbours to the south are in large part dependent.

Is my
right hon. friend quite sure of that statement? I understand that magazine paper bears a duty of 40 per cent in the United States, and that very little of it is exported to the United States from Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I cannot give
the particulars, but I am making a statement which I think is generally accurate. There is always the possibility of conditions changing with respect to importations of paper, and at any moment the American magazines may become more dependent on Canadian paper than ever. To the extent to which that is the case anything which will restrict the sale of these publications will I believe be injurious.
May I point out another feature, one which to my mind is the most important of any. So far as the well-to-do are concerned, the difference of a few cents on a magazine or periodical would be a matter -of no concern. This change will not affect the homes of those who are already in fortunate circumstances. However if there is one right above another which the poor man is entitled to have respected, it is that he shall be able to get at the lowest possible cost his sources of knowledge and inspiration, and that there shall be available to him immediately, and through the libraries of the country anything in the nature of helpful reading material and literature. I venture to say that in many humble homes in this land the first sacrifice which because of additional cost will have to be made as a result of the general depression will be magazines and periodicals which come from across the line into our country and which have served as* sources of information and inspiration in the different homes of Canada. Particularly will that be so in many of the more remote parts of the country and in the libraries of institutions not supported by the state, but which depend upon private contributions and grants to secure their different publications.
I do not wish to specialize, because as I 3ay if between now and September 30, was it?-

speechtext: September 1.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, Septemoer 1. If between now and September 1, the Prime Minister strikes off the list of the original resolution all the publications of any
importance, of course my objection would be wholly removed. I submit however that there again my right hon. friend has made a mistake characteristic of him in that at the very start he attempts to do everything in a wholesale manner, and after he has shaken up as much as possible the existing order of things he endeavours to remedy the situation by making changes and eliminations. I do not think that is a good policy for industry', nor in this instance is it good for the social and literary life of the country. With respect to taxes in other directions his action has been definitely harmful to the financial and industrial structure of the country.
I do submit that my right hon. friend in the first instance might well have gone through the list of magazines and periodicals and have come to the house with a list of those publications which because of their pernicious or salacious nature, he thought should be prohibited. He might have prohibited, with the consent of all, publications of a type that we do not wish to have in Canada. So far as pernicious and salacious literature is concerned I am entirely at one with the Prime Minister in a desire to prevent its spread. I believe, however, that the better way to deal with that sort of literature is the method which has been adopted in the past, namely to have some known form of censorship which under the minister will be responsible for the decisions made, and have all such publications banned entirely. I would go a step further and say that there are publications in our own country which might well be suppressed and which should not be permitted to find a place on vendors' stalls. So far as that class of literature is concerned, I am entirely in accord with my right hon. friend in his desire for its suppression.
With respect to all other classes of literature however I think the people themselves should be left to choose for themselves what they may wish to read. As I said to my right hon. friend the other day, I do not doubt the sincerity of his desire to be a protector of this nation with respect to what people shall pay, what they shall eat and what they shall wear-and now, with respect to what they shall read and think-but I do submit that the people themselves are much more capable of judging what they should read, what they have the right to read and what they wish to read than is my right hon. friend.
That voices not only my own feelings but those I believe of all hon. members who sit on this side of the house. The proposed tax is one upon art, because after all art is a

result of the expression of ideas. It is a tax upon invention, because invention is the offspring of ideas. To my way of thinking it is more or less of a tax upon everything which makes for progress.
I suppose we shall have to wait until September to see the extent of this tax upon the literature and periodicals coming into Canada from the United States and other countries. I know there is something to be said in connection with what the Prime Minister has expressed with regard to advertising. If advertising from other countries coming into Canada can be taxed in Canada, I think it should be taxed to the degree the same kind of advertising is taxed in Canada. I am afraid, however, my right hon. friend will find that not only will he fail to raise the revenue he hopes to raise from this particular source of taxation, but he will lose a considerable amount of money in revenue, and in the end will be obliged to cancel a good deal of what he is attempting to do at the moment. As 1 have said we will wait until September to see what he allows to come into the country. In this connection may I say to him I do hope he will act from the Liberal point of view and not the Conservative when he considers what constitutes scientific, educational and religious publications, which, I believe, are the three types of publications to be exempted. May I point out that While many imported magazines are not distinctly religious, nor scientific nor educational in character, vet in the broad sense of the words they are all three, because they are, to an appreciable degree, a composite of the thought of a nation.

Mr. Chairman, with respect
to people living in remote districts away from news stands who subscribe for these magazines, what arrangements are made for the clearance through customs every week as they come in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not apprehend any
clearance will be made through customs. The proprietors will pay the duties before the magazines come into Canada, or as they pass the boundary.
I am sorry I was not in k position to hand this amendment to my right hon. friend before the house met. As a matter of fact I was not able to complete it until just before lunch. The officials of the department and myself were busy all morning with the amendment because it was desired that it should operate with as little inconvenience as possible to everybody. I think my right hon. friend has not quite appreciated the full importance of the change. It was because of certain ob-

jections made to the Minister of Finance and the government of the day becoming the judges of what people should read that it has been dealt with in the manner indicated by the changes themselves. It can be no longer said that the governor in council will determine what is religious, what is scientific or what is educational. The matter is placed upon another basis altogether. Particularly there are three classes which we have to consider: First, that class, with respect to the importation of which into the country there is no question raised at all. Those are the magazines that supply food for thought. I will not mention them by name because that might be taken as being in some sense an erroneous thing to do. But they are the great monthly periodicals, they are the digests of thought that contain very little or no advertising matter. Those will continue to come in free. Then there is the second class, which is mainly of a type that we would prefer not to have. It divides itself in turn into two great subdivisions: (a) those that are principally advertising material; and (b) those that contain reading of such a type that it is better out of the country than in it, and as to the advisability of its importation into this country the right hon. gentleman agrees entirely with myself and I with him.
Now I put this to my right hon. friend. If in the country of origin it is thought desirable to tax the advertising in those journals or periodicals or publications, the reading matter of which cannot be excelled, when they are also carrying advertising according to their own statements that is referable to Canada, why should not we also receive from them some revenue? Every argument that my right hon. friend has made as to taxation imposed upon thought and literature applies to the country of origin, only the tax is higher there. The tax, however, is-absorbed largely by the publishers in the country of origin, and we believe that in most instances the two cents and five cents will be absorbed by the publishers here. For instance, the journal or periodical sold at five cents in the United States is sold at ten cents here-we will say it is sold in New York at five cents and at the same price in San Francisco-and the postal charge to California is seven cents. If the journal is sold at ten cents here, why should not that extra five cents be absorbed by the publisher? That would be an illustration of what I mean. Owing to the fact that we have no zone system in Canada in connection with postal rates-and personally at the moment I think with our limited population it would be very undesirable to have

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
chat, and in this respect I agree with the former administration-we cannot secure revenue from this advertising through the postal department, and this is the only method by which, so far as we can see, it is possible to secure revenue.
I will not repeat myself. We are desirous of causing as little inconvenience as possible, and therefore our desire was to approach this problem not in the reckless, ruthless manner described by my right hon. friend, but rather to approach it from the standpoint of moderation, and a charge of two cents or five cents cannot be said to be immoderate when in the country of origin the advertising material is taxed seven cents.
Is that five cents per pound, or per issue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Per copy in this instance; in that instance it is seven cents a pound, but in many cases the journals in question weigh a pound and a quarter and sometimes a pound and a half. My right hon. friend perhaps has misunderstood me. There was no revenue derived from this source before, except the revenue from the postal department in connection with the transmission of these periodicals through the mails. This is new revenue, whatever it may be, much or little.
Might I also point out that the efforts to secure some revenue from this source is the more warranted because in the very journals themselves they state that by reason of there being American branch industries or factories in this country, the advertising carried in their journals, which have a circulation of 1,400,000 copies per issue-that is the sum total of the single issues of the most important of these journals-this advertising medium in this country-Canada-is so important and their rates are so reasonable that they can cater to the Canadian demand, although they publish abroad and make no contribution to our wellbeing, except the contribution I have mentioned through the postal department.
Now my right hon. friend has raised four or five points that are worthy of consideration. He said, first of all, thought is universal, and there should be no restriction on its transmission. With respect to that I think it will be found that there is no departure from the general rule in this country with regard to the publications in question more than there is in the country of their origin, and the great magazines and digests that supply the seed-thought for so many will still enter without payment of duty. I think, so far as is reason-22110-247
ably possible, we have endeavoured to meet that very situation to which the right hon. gentleman referred.
Dealing with the next point, namely, the question of the interference with authors and making it impossible for them to sell the product of their brain, their mind, their thought, their pen, I can only say this: I do not believe, despite what the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) has said of their already having done so, that any great, reputable magazine or publication will decline to accept the products of the mind and thought of a Canadian because the Dominion of Canada sees fit to place upon the entrance into this country of the medium through which that thought is disseminated a lesser tax than that which is imposed in the country of origin. I have yet to believe that that is so. On the other hand, I am inclined to think it will have the effect of stimulating the demand for the product of the mind and thought of Canadians.
On the newsprint item I was rather amazed at the right hon. gentleman. It is one of the interesting circumstances to which many of us have alluded that while the great republic [DOT] to the south permits our pulp and paper and newsprint to enter free into their markets because they need the raw material, if we tried to sell them a pound of magazine paper we would find ourselves confronted with a forty per cent tariff. So that so far as selling them magazine paper is concerned, we practically sell them none, nor is it possible for us to do so. But with respect to pulp-I think that perhaps is what the right hon. gentleman meant-there are importations into the United States from this country to be worked up into magazine paper, and I am bound to say that some quantities of that pulp have been reimported into this country in the form of the finished article. But I do not think they will cease to buy our pulp, because we have taken some of the profits from the publisher in the form of a contribution to the revenues of the country that transports the magazine thousands of miles at the same rate as it does ten miles, there being no zone system here as there is there. So for a great publication of one hundred pages, of which fifty is advertising matter, we in Canada, transporting it through the mails for ten miles, would receive exactly the same sum as for transmitting it from Niagara Falls to Vancouver or Victoria. This remedies that condition and provides that the principle which applies in the country of origin, namely, the imposition of a tax based upon a zone system shall be recognized

In a general way I must endorse what was said by the leader of the opposition. With regard to the advertising, I am not sure that this end could not be reached in some other way than by interfering with the reading material. As I see it- and I, together with the other members of the committee, have not had a chance to study the modification proposed-the literature must be divided into three broad classes.
First there is the objectionable literature, which undoubtedly should be shut out entirely. The whole point there is what is objectionable, and I have very serious doubts as to whether we are wise to entrust censorship powers to a department. I know that at present an officer of the department reads books and rejects a certain number, and there are certain instances in which I find myself somewhat of a different view from that of the censor, if I might call him such. On the whole I have no particular quarrel with the work he has done, but it does seem to me that we should set up some sort of appeal board so that one man, unknown to the general public, sitting in his own closed office, should not have the right to shut out literature that might be adjudged perfectly decent by a great many people throughout the country. I think if we must have a censorship we

should have some sort of board of appeal to which might be referred matters in dispute. I would respectfully make that suggestion to the Prime Minister for his consideration when-he is considering future arrangements. There are certain matters verging on religion which are very objectionable to some parts of the community but which are considered quite innocuous by other sections. There are certain matters relative to sex on which certain members of the community have very strong ideas while other members look at the subject in a very different light. I do not think that in these matters we should leave the decision entirely in the hands of one man, however good he may be.
I am not very clear with respect to the second class of literature I have in mind; I refer to what we generally regard as to the better and more educational magazines. The Prime Minister has said that all thought-provoking magazines will be permitted free entry. There are certain magazines which are very popular with a good many of the women in our homes, such as Good Housekeeping and the Ladies Home Journal. I do not know whether or not these would be admitted free. I do not read them a great [DOT] deal, but I think they contain a good many thought-provoking articles. I know a good many housewives have been accustomed to read these magazines for the information they obtain therefrom. It is true that these magazines cany a good deal of advertising material, and as far as I am concerned I think there is a good deal of nonsense in them, but at the same time I believe thousands upon thousands of women across this country welcome magazines of this kind, and I do not think they should be excluded by heavy taxation. I am afraid they will not come under the thought-provoking classification of the Prime Minister.
There is another class about which I am not clear; I refer to magazines such as Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. These again are magazines which are welcomed in our homes by our boys, who are very keen to read what has been done in the way of invention and what are the latest discoveries of science. I do not know whether or not these would be classed as educational. If they are not so classed I think they should be regarded as such. It is true that they contain an enormous amount of advertising; I have often wished that they did not contain so much, but along with that advertising there is a great amount of good material which appeals to our boys, so I think that they should be admitted free.

Then there are those other magazines such as The Literary Digest, The Atlantic, The New Republic, The Nation, The Forum, American Foreign Affairs and a number of others. I do not know whether they come under the Prime Minister's classification of thought-provoking magazines. I find some of those quite informative and thought-provoking, and it seems to me that decidedly they should be admitted to this country and given as wide a circulation as possible. At this stage of our development, with only ten million people in our coimtry, of whom three million speak French as their mother tongue and two or three million more who have come recently from Europe and have not acquired a good knowledge of the English language, and hence are not capable of reading magazines of that kind, I submit that the English speaking constituency in Canada is altogether too limited for us to hope to publish magazines of that class in this country. I know we have a Canadian Forum published in Toronto and several quarterly magazines such as the Queens Quarterly, the Dalhousie Review and others connected with the universities which are doing excellent work, but we cannot hope to have published in Canada those semi-popular magazines which deal with economic and political questions. They have a hard enough time to keep them going in the United States; it is only because they have people who are philanthropically inclined and who come to the rescue from time to time with large donations that certain of these magazines and papers keep alive even in the United States, where the reading public is so much larger than in Canada. I would hope that magazines of this class would be admitted free. Here again I suppose the difficulty is that many of these magazines carry considerable advertising matter. None the less they are decidedly educational in character.
There is, in addition, that other class of magazine which I think the Prime Minister will agree we should prefer not to have our people read. They are for entertainment and recreational purposes. Some of them do not provide a very high type of entertainment, but I do not know that we should try to exclude them. If our people have not been educated to the point where they themselves reject such magazines; if they are still at the grade 3 or grade 4 stage of development, where they like to read these things, I do not know that we should shut them out. It must be remembered, after all, that most of our people like to see the movies, which, on the whole, do not demand a very great deal of

intelligence, so why should we attempt to keep out literature of this kind when we let in the movies which appeal to intelligence of the same degree of development? I do not know that they appeal to any lower ideals than do the movies. I do not know why people who may be said to have somewhat highbrow notions should undertake to educate forcibly the great masses of the people, and why they should refuse to allow the people to read that which they like to read for purposes of recreation. There are many people who like to read those magazines which many of us do not regard as being of the highest educational character, but I think we should be very cautious in taking away from any class of people that which is of great interest to them. I protest against this particular way of raising revenue; I think almost any other way would be more desirable than the imposition of a tax on the magazines which serve either the educational or recreational needs of the people.

Mr. Chairman, judging from the amendments which have been moved, I am not sure whether or not I should protest against this item. I attended a convention in Wetaskiwin riding a few weeks ago at which very strenuous objections were taken to the tax on magazines. However, as I understand the amendments, most of these objections have been removed. I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Woodsworth) that it would be a very difficult thing for either a department or the governor in council to judge what literature is religious, scientific, or educational in character. This amendment removes this necessity, and to that extent I think it will be very welcome.
As to the classification of literature which will come under this tax, I agree with both the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that it would be better if a certain class

The original application of the M.P.A.-
That is the Magazine Publishers Association.
-was for a tax on the advertising contents of foreign periodicals. It was made about one year ago, and since the presentation of that case and the second hearing of it, we have had some opportunity to make a survey of public and parliamentary opinion in regard to our request.
Our conclusion is that, while we have the sympathy of all Canadians, public and parliamentary, and while they think it would be desirable to restrict the importation of some foreign periodicals, at the same time it would be a dangerous thing to place a tax on reading matter. We take the ground that this is a matter of public interest; for after all, while our case is one of equity and justice, the aspect that commands particular attention is the public welfare. The only obstacle in the way of greater service which will make for the prosperity of the farming community, the working people, the consumers of Canada generally, and which will promote a true Canadian spirit, is the cost of publishing.

The publishers ask for 99 per cent drawback of duty on printing plant and machinery, art work for editorial purposes, engravings for printing in two or more colours, etc., and the removal of sales tax.

The third motive would be that of protection, and high protection at that. May I in that connection point out that it will not be the Canadian magazines that will be protected. I doubt very much if the magazines coming into Canada from the United States or other countries interfere to any considerable extent with publications of a like character in this country. Then let my right hon. friend be quite frank about it and say that again it is to protect the manufacturer in this country, and that he is going to protect him by closing the eyes, so far as that is possible, of the Canadian people to opportunities to buy elsewhere at less cost or to have any knowledge of the kind of articles that are being produced in another country which might serve the purposes of the consumer equally well if not better. That to my mind is the really mischievous feature of the whole proposal. It is a further restriction of trade,, it is again an effort to further the interests of a particular class at the expense of the great body of consumers with respect to what they may wish to wear, what they may wish to eat, wherewithal they may wish to be housed and clothed, and the means by which their various other needs and satisfactions are to be met. I think that is the real explanation of it, and if it is not, I should be glad if my right hon. friend would make the matter clear.

My conviction is that the tax will be paid principally by the publishers.
Thirdly, the right hon. gentleman has suggested that we are endeavouring to protect the manufacturers of this country. I pointed out that the basis of this whole provision is found in these words, "which, by reason of their advertising content, are subject in the country of origin to zone rates of postage based upon such advertising content." Not being able to reach them through the Post Office Department without changing our whole scheme of postal imposts, we are reaching them in this way, but at a somewhat lesser rate than that which they would pay if the postal charges were similar to those in the United States. I pointed out that in the United States the first zone, which is up to 150 miles, makes a tax against the publisher, which he has to pay at the post office where the magazine is posted, of li cents per pound; if it goes 300 miles he pays 2 cents a pound, and that is in addition to the ordinary postal rate; it is a charge by way of surtax. If it travels 600 miles, the charge is 3 cents per pound, and if it travels 1,000 miles, the charge is 4 cents per pound, and so on up to 7 cents per pound. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are many difficulties about prohibition in a matter of that kind. I could tell the hon. gentleman, if I went into the international aspect, of features that would make him realize that previous governments when the matter was brought to their attention did not take the action of prohibition because of the difficulty, but every state concedes to every other state the right of censorship as to the kind of literature that should come within its borders. But there is a kind that lies on the border line, not being on the one hand, clearly such as should be excluded because of violation of ethics or morals and matters of that kind, and the convictions of the people, ye't on the other hand exerting the very influences that work so insidiously upon the formation of character. Hon. members in this house are more concerned than I because they have given hostages to fortune and are concerned as to what their children's attitude towards life shall be. I say however one of the problems that every thoughtful man and woman in Canada must be thinking about is: What will be the attitude of mind and the character of the rising generation which every Sunday is permitted to read that form of comic strip? Children seven, eight, nine and ten years of age are permitted to read those strips which magnify every device to which youngsters might resort to cheat, to circumvent their elders and to make them think that to lie is a virtue. I say that is one of the problems this country must seriously consider for the welfare of the generation of manhood and womanhood which is marching forward, the first generation in Canada which has been subjected indiscriminately to that influence.
We have not sought prohibition in this connection for many reasons, and I want my hon. friend from Weyburn to know that the publishers did not seek it; I know of no man who asked that it be done. The government believes it should be done; I believe it should be done; every member of the administration believes it should be done not because we are censors, not because we arrogate to ourselves any virtues we do not possess, but because for the moment being trustees of power we must exercise its sway over what is best for the people of this country and the new generation of manhood and womanhood marching up.

That is the position. There is no desire to protect industry or manufacturers or anybody else, except the Canadian people, in the broad and general acceptance of that term. The weekly average of all American magazines is 1,400,000 copies, or about 4 per cent of the whole circulation because, as is well known, the total circulations are enormous. Total prohibition is the only remedy that can be applied.
The censor will remain

Does not my hon. friend know that the easiest way to get over the censor, and over any provisions looking to prohibition, is to change the name of the magazine and bring it into Canada under a slightly altered title? If there is the mere prohibition of a magazine of a salacious character having a certain title; if it is known and prohibited under that title, it is the easiest thing in the world for the publisher in the United States to change the title and the general make-up of the cover and send back the magazine, and there is nothing to stop it from coming in. The same thing is true of a censorship. When magazines of this type are prohibited the name is changed over night and it comes back again.

It is known that that system is practised, but we have the censorship for that purpose. This undesirable literature is coming in at the present time, we see it being sold in cigar stores, and if it is to be kept out, a proper system of censorship will have to be established. I do not believe that any system of taxation will prevent it coming to this country. There is a certain element who like to read this sort of literature, and a tax of fifteen cents per copy will not curtail the circulation in Canada. speechtext: Not at all.

I do not quite agree with the contention that the idea of this legislation is to keep out undesirable magazines. Even although they are kept out, things come in over the air which are more injurious than the magazines themselves. We have but to turn on our radio and we are flooded with the very stuff that is contained in these undesirable magazines and newspapers. We turn on the radio Sunday morning, before the church services and we hear Uncle Ned or Uncle Bill taking page after page of these newspapers of the Chicago type and telling about the escapades of the Katzenjammer kids and other characters. He goes through the newspaper page after page, and that is what our children listen to on Sunday morning. It might just as well be admitted that this legislation is for the purpose of raising the revenue needed by the country in an emergency, and not as a means of censorship. There are ways of evading any censorship, and the public is appealed to in one way or another. This is not the correct way to instil in the minds of our children the appreciation of better things. Another danger will be that these people may come right into our own country. In fact, they are here already, publishing these undesirable magazines, and certain types of pictorials. If we object on moral grounds let us go after this thing vigorously. I approve of the taxation being placed on some of these periodicals because we need revenue and protection. I do not know that I have anything further to say only just to protest against the argument being used that the morals of the country are being protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext:
The amendment under discussion at the last sitting on this bill was the proposed addition of a further section whereby the coming into force of this act could be postponed by order in council, the purpose being to withhold the coming into force of the act until a sufficient number of nations had ratified the conventions so as to put them into effect; otherwise, in the perhaps somewhat hypothetical case of five nations failing to ratify the convention, this would be law in Canada but not so in a majority of the other maritime nations. The discussion took place in regard to the wording of that amendment. The wording is about the same as that of the similar section in the bill now before the British House of Commons, which section reads:
Provided that His Majesty may from time to time by order in council postpone the coming into operation of this part of this act for such period not exceeding on any occasion of postponement one year, as may be specified in the order.
Since the committee rose, I have discussed the matter with my officials, especially with Mr. Johnston, my deputy minister, who was the representative of Canada at those conventions; also with officials of the Department of Justice and with Doctor Skelton of the Department of External Affairs. We came to the conclusion that we should substitute another section which is perhaps clearer and which I shall read to the committee:
This act or any portion thereof shall come into operation on a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette.
I think this substitute section is clearer and will meet the purpose.

So all that is necessary is to deposit our ratification, and if five ratifications have been deposited before July 1, 1931, the convention will come into force on that date, and if five ratifications have not been deposited by that date the convention will come into force three months after the date on which the fifth ratification is deposited. So I see no reason whatever for this amendment. It is just as objectionable as the previous amendment because it leaves it to the governor in council to say when our ratification shall be deposited, and that may hold up not merely this country but other countries which have ratified the convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext: The reason why we want to delay the coming into force of this law in Canada even after five countries have ratified the convention is that we do not want to have this law in force in Canada if adjoining countries have not ratified the convention, because in that case our boats would be discriminated against. This convention will be in force only in those countries which have ratified it. If we ratified it without any clause such as the one suggested1, we would be bound by the convention and other countries close to us which had not ratified would not be bound. So, after long consideration with our officials, we thought it better tp postpone the coming into force of this law in Canada until adjoining countries had also ratified the convention.

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT LONDON
speechtext:
In that case it would be better to change the title of the bill, "The Safety of Life at Sea and Load Line Conventions Act, 1931." If we are going to make
provision for the safety of life at sea, and if the convention in its wisdom laid down that ratification by five countries should be sufficient to bring it into force, I see no virtue in holding up the convention indefinitely until some countries adjacent to us have ratified it. We should set the example, along with four other countries, by depositing our ratification immediately with the British government. If the convention itself is necessary for the safety of life at sea, we should not allow the matter of competition with other nations which may not be as humane in this matter as we are, to prevent its coming into force. The minister himself stated that there was no reason for deferring the convention. As a matter of fact, it is violating article 65 to delay ratification any further. Article 65 lays down the requirements necessary to give effect to the convention.

speechtext:
While this bill contains only fourteen comparatively short sections, it is really a very long and intricate bill covering over 200 pages, and I venture to assert that there is not a man in the house who has even a working acquaintance with the bill or would be capable of passing a schoolboy's examination on it. I should like to know why this bill was not sent to the marine committee, where there would have been at least some opportunity to investigate it. It contains another feature which I never saw in any bill presented to this house before, and that is that page after page contains deletion of words or sentences struck out. Who struck them out? Did we authorize the striking out? Is there any record of that striking out? Is there anything to prevent anybody, after this bill passes, making a few more deletions and saying: That is the bill as you passed it? I do not believe the regulations were read or even called here. We probably passed them by passing a section to the effect that the governor in council shall have power to make regulations. The house does not know the first thing about this bill. It should have gone to the marine committee. What is that committee for but for matters of this kind?
Since the Minister of Justice has in some sense opened up preceding sections by giving notice of an amendment which covers several sections that we have already passed, it might be permissible for me to ask this further question. Section 3 of the bill reads:
This act shall not apply to ships while engaged on voyages between Canada and the United States of America on any lakes or rivers.

I think probably, speaking without positive knowledge, that the percentage of loss of life on the great lakes on a given number of ships is as great as on the Atlantic, which is covered by this convention, yet we are not going to make it apply in our own waters, or waters contiguous to our territory, on which are boats manned by crews of our own nationality and where the waters, especially in the fall, are very dangerous. We do not put this provision in. Does not charity begin at home; does not safety begin at home? These are things which illustrate the fact that we know nothing about this bill, and I would suggest that even at this late date it should be sent to a committee so that some expert opinions may be heard in connection with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine
subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT LONDON

subtopic: BILL TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT LONDON

speechtext:
On the first reading I
explained to some extent the purpose of this bill. It is not intended to disturb the Pension Act passed at the last regular session except as to one principle and in one direction. I wish to amend section one of the bill by inserting before the words "section nine" in line four the words "subsection one."

Pension Act

subtopic: INCREASE IN MEMBERSHIP OF PENSION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
I do not rise for the purpose of taking exception to the bill. If I had any complaint to register it would be that other amendments are required in addition to those presented by the minister to do justice to the returned men. In saying this I do not wish for one moment to criticize the minister or his administration. As a matter of fact my experience has been that he and his officials are conducting the department-which is one of the most important, and certainly the most overworked of all the departments of government-as satisfactorily as possible under the circumstances. In the legislation we passed a year ago it was thought we had established the principle of giving to the returned soldier the benefit of the doubt in all circumstances, but unfortunately we now find the ex-service man in certain instances not given the benefit of the doubt at all, in fact in my judgment he is very little better off than he was before the said legislation was enacted. To illustrate this perhaps I cannot do better than state an actual case which was heard in my own county. A pensioner's case was tried by two commissioners who after hearing all the evidence, at the conclusion of their deliberations-the court sat for a couple of days and heard other cases besides the one with which I am dealing-rendered a decision in favour of the applicant receiving a pension. They said to him:	We have heard your case and
on the evidence presented have decided that you are entitled to a pension; we are submitting a report to this effect to the proper authorities and in due course your case will go to the Board of Pension Commissioners for assessment and pension. In addition to the two commissioners, witnesses and tribunal officials there were present expert medical men and, counsel for the department-the devil's advocate-and the returned soldier's advocate. While I did not hear the evidence adduced in this particular case, I heard the evidence in other cases before this same tribunal, and I am convinced that the court was conducted in a fair, judicial and logical manner and their verdict was a good one. An appeal was carried by the devil's advocate to the pension appeal court where the decision of the pension tribunal was reversed, and the man will not now receive a pension, after having been instructed by the pension tribunal that he would.
Now, I contend that having a year ago decided that in every case the returned man was to receive the benefit of the doubt, this judgment of the pension appeal court in reversing the former decision is a direct viola-[Mr. MacLaren. I
tion of that principle, because certainly not only a reasonable but a judicial doubt was established by the fact that one court decided in the applicants favour; and this is not the only case where such a doubt has been established with disastrous results. Such an anomaly should not be allowed to continue, for the very excellent reason that it works a grave injustice to the returned man who is seeking justice, and it is not in accordance with the principle, that all ex-service men were to be given the benefit of the doubt, which we thought we had established by the legislation enacted over a year ago. I think ir. is a proper suggestion to make to the minister that if possible some legislation should be brought forward to remove that anomaly.

subtopic: INCREASE IN MEMBERSHIP OF PENSION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Unfortunately the case referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland is not the only case of that kind. A tribunal sat in New Glasgow, and one forenoon was occupied with one particular case. I heard the evidence, and the chairman of the tribunal stated that the decision would be rendered the following morning. The decision was given, in favour of the applicant. Shortly afterwards the case was appealed, and after some weeks of delay the appeal was heard and the judgment of the tribunal sustained. So far as I am aware that man has not yet received his pension. That sort of thing is not creditable to this country; it is not 'the sort of treatment we thought we were according the returned men when we passed this legislation a year ago.

Mr. ERRICK F. WILLIS (Souris) moved that Bill No. 118, to incorporate Service Loan and Finance Corporation, be recommitted to
the select standing committee on banking and commerce.

Mr. Speaker, when this matter was first referred to by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) I took exception, and I desire to take a few minutes to show why I think the bill should not be again referred to 22110-248i
the select standing committee on banking and commerce. As hon. members know this is a Senate bill which was passed and forwarded to the House of Commons. When bills come from the Senate perhaps hon. members in this house do not give to them as careful thought as is given to bills originating in this house, the usual practice being to send such bills to the committee for consideration. Hon. members probably have not read this bill very closely, and perhaps are unaware of the nature of the legislation. I will refer to one or two clauses to which objection was taken by the committee, and my contention is that no matter what explanation is given by the hon. member for West York, it is quite unlikely that a further reference to the committee will accomplish any definite result. The bill was before the committee, it was considered very carefully, and received the support of but a few hon. members. The bill was thoroughly explained by counsel for the company; it was also explained by the superintendent of insurance, so that there was no doubt left in the minds of the committee as to what the bill meant or as to its specific provisions.
Paragraph (b) of subsection 1 of section 5 of the bill reads:
The company may throughout Canada-
(b) notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act, or in the Money Lenders Act, or in paragraph (c) of section sixty-three of the Loan Companies Act-
That is to say, the other acts which govern the operations of such a company are set aside and special provisions are made in this bill to give the company concerned almost unlimited powers to charge those who borrow from it. It is permitted to:
(i)	lend money secured by assignment of choses-in-action, chattel mortgages or such other evidence of indebtedness as the company may require, and may charge interest thereon at the rate of not more than seven per centum per annum, and may on all loans deduct the interest in advance and provide for repayments in weekly, monthly or other uniform repayments: Provided that the borrower shall have the right to repay the loan at any time before the due date, and, on such repayment being made, to receive a refund of such portion of the interest paid in advance as has not been earned, except a sum equal to the interest for three months,
The following is the most objectionable paragraph:
(ii)	charge, in addition to interest as aforesaid, for all expenses which have been necessarily and in good faith incurred by the company in making or renewing a loan authorized by the next preceding sub-paragraph (i), including all expenses for inquiry and investigation into the character and circumstances of the

Loan and Finance Corporation
borrower, his endorsers, co-makers or sureties, for taxes, correspondence and professional advice, and for all necessary documents and papers, two per centum upon the principal sum loaned.
The powers given to the company to make extra charges in this connection are almost unlimited. We cannot even imagine the extent to which the company may go in this respect. These were the chief objections to the bill. The committee believed that greater powers than should be granted to any company were provided for in this legislation, and they objected to the setting aside of the Money Lenders Act, the Loan Companies Act and the Interest Act merely to give this company special power. Further, it was pointed out by the Superintendent of Insurance that this company is already operating under a provincial charter. If it wishes to extend its business into other provinces, all that is required is for it to secure licences from the provinces which it desires to enter. It may then carry on its business there, so that even if this bill should not be proceeded with further, the company would not suffer any serious disadvantage. The House of Commons, however, by rejecting this measure, will not be regarded as being remiss in its duty to protect the public interest, and if a provincial government wishes to grant a licence to carry on a business of that sort, that is its concern.
It may be pointed out further that the bill gives this particular company, power to lend money to a class of people in Canada who would not be able to borrow from the banks or from other money lending institutions. The contention is that people of that class have very little or no credit, at least not sufficient for the banks to recognize them. It was argued by those supporting the bill that if it were not passed we would be doing an injustice to that particular class. The answer to that will be apparent to everyone. This is a class of people, who, it is alleged, have no credit with the banks. Therefore, in all fairness, that class of people, if they borrow, should receive a lower rate of interest than any other class. But by this bill we are providing legislation which will permit the company to charge them at least 17 per cent. To ask the poorest class in the community, with practically no credit at the banks, if they are forced by circumstances to secure a loan from this company, to pay 17 per cent is, I submit, not helping that class at all. That is usury of the very worst kind, and if parliament cannot do anything better for that class than pass legislation of such a character, we had better not legislate at all.

Moreover, I do not think it is good business, especially at this stage of the session, to duplicate our work. In the banking and commerce committee we considered this bill to the best of our ability, and it was defeated in that committee. I cannot see any reason why an exception should be made of this bill by sending it back for the reconsideration of the select standing committe on banking and commerce.

I wish heartily to support the contention put forward by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) with regard to bis criticism of this bill. Only the other dlay, when it was before us in the banking and commerce committee, it was most thoroughly discussed. The legal advisers who were advocating the bill had ample time to put forward their case, and I was quite surprised when the sponsor of the bill rose in his place in the house the other day and asked permission that it be placed again on the order paper after it had been defeated' in the banking and commerce committee, giving as his reason for wishing to have it reconsidered that he was not present at the banking and commerce committee when the bill was brought uip, and that possibly he could have presented the case with different results. The hon. member knew he was not going to be at the banking and commerce committee that morning; he knew the bill was up for discussion and he had made full arrangements to have it presented. An hon. member to your right, Mr. Speaker, had full charge of the bill; he informed the committee that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) could not be present, and that the latter had asked him to take his place and present the bill for him. I can assure the hon. member for West York that the bill was put forward very aibly by the hon. member who took bis place. Therefore, in that regard he has no reason for asking the house to reconsider the bill and have it sent back to the committee-simply because he was not present the other morning to stand sponsor for it. That was the only reason I heard him give.
The powers given to this company, the Service Loan and Finance Corporation, are, as outlined by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, very large. We were led, before reading the bill, to believe that the main security on which this corporation would lend money was simply that of two signers, but I find the following in section 5 of the bill:
The company may throughout Canada-
(a) buy, sell, deal in and lend money on the security of conditional sales agreements, lien notes, hire purchase agreements, chattel mort-

Loan and Finance Corporation
gages, trade paper, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, bills of exchange and choses-in-action; and may receive and accept from the makers, vendors or transferors thereof guarantees or other security for the performance and payment thereof and may enforce such guarantees and realize on such security;
The privileges given to the company in this bill are second only to those given to our banking institutions. If anyone wanting to borrow money has any security at all to offer and is a good risk, our present banking facilities are available. As was mentioned by the previous speaker, the superintendent of insurance when asked what rate of interest could be charged under this bill, although it calls for only 7 per cent, informed the committee that in view of the many provisos whereby the company can charge a little here and a little there, and take advantage of the borrower by demanding repayment weekly or monthly, together with the privilege of discounting. the rate of interest would amount to not less than 17 or 18 per cent. In some twenty-three years of my life I have seen what happened to men who borrowed at no higher rates than 8 or 9 or 10 per cent. I have seen many a business eventually go to the wall and many and many a family driven from home. I have seen people who at one time had great hopes of success struggle on for perhaps a quarter of a lifetime only to be compelled in the end to go into bankruptcy or worse, simply because of the high rate of interest charged on the money they borrowed. If that is the case when interest rates are 8 or 10 per cent, what can we expect to be the result when the interest rate is 17 or 18 peT cent? It is terrible to think of. Some say that these companies are working very well, and probably they are so far as the shareholders are concerned, but I cannot imagine for a moment how they can be working well in any respect so far as the borrower - is concerned. If a 'borrower is so down and out that he cannot get accommodation either through his life insurance, or through a bank or through a mortgage company or from friends, if he has not two good backers, then in any event if he has the security that this bill calls for, he should be able to get accommodation through the various channels at present available.
As the hon. member for Wetaskiwin pointed out, section 5, subsection 1 (b) of this bill provides:
(b) notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act or in the Money Lenders Act, or in paragraph (c) of section 63 of the Loan Companies Act-
The company may;
(i) lend money secured by assignment of choses-in-action, chattel mortgages or such other
evidence of indebtedness as the company may require, and may charge interest thereon at the rate of not more than seven per centum per annum, and may on all loans deduct the interest in advance and provide for repayments in weekly, monthly or other uniform repayments: provided that the borrower shall have the right to repay the loan at any time before the due date, and, on such repayment being made, to receive a refund of such portion of the interest paid in advance as has not been earned, except a sum equal to the interest for three months,
So even when the company refunds the interest that has not been earned on account of the loan being repaid before the due date, they make the proviso: Oh yes, we will refund the interest, but we intend to keep three months' unearned interest.
This bill, if it means anything at all, means short term loans. The argument was put up 'to us the other day that money might be suddenly required to pay the expenses of a doctor in ease of sickness, or hospital expenses, that the money would be wanted for a short time. If that is the object of the bill, why provide that, the company may retain three months' unearned interest? Although the bill at first sight looks quite harmless in calling for a rate of 7 per cent, when you take into consideration its many provisos allowing the company to charge for looking into the bona fides of the co-signers, into the value of securities, and the proviso that the lender may deduct the interest before the loan is made, and may make various charges here and there, we find according to the testimony of the superintendent of insurance himself that the rate the unfortunate borrower would have to pay is not 7 per cent, but between 17 and 18 per cent.
How does the hon. mem-bre figure it at 17 or 18 per cent? It is 7 per cent, plus 2 per cent for investigations.

I shall have to refer the hon. member to the superintendent of insurance, who, I would say without hesitation, is one of the ablest mathematicians and civil servants that Canada is proud, to have working for her. After carefully looking over the bill he came to the conclusion and stated to the banking and commerce committee that the rate in all would amount to 17 or 18 per cent. That is all we have to work on. It may be more than that, but he put it at 17 to 18 per cent. That makes this bill nothing more or less than a usurer's bill of the worst sort, and I do think, Mr. Speaker, that it is not in the interests of the people of Canada for this parliament to pass it. I think the committee did right in turning down the principle of the bilL I

Loan and Finance Corporation
support the chairman of the committee entirely in the report that he has made to the house, and I very much regret to see that this bill has been put back on the order paper.
Do I understand that this company already has a provincial charter? I am not a member of the banking and commerce committee, and I ask for information.
Yes.
Do they already enjoy these privileges under provincial legislation?
I do not know whether they have exactly the same privileges under the provincial legislation, but I have never seen quite such a raw bill as this presented to the house.
I was simply wondering whether they were carrying on raw practices under provincial legislation.

Even if they have these rights under provincial legislation, I do not think we should soil our hands in supporting such cruelty as to allow a usurer to penalize unfortunate borrowers to the extent allowed under this bill.
Mr. ERRICK F. WILLIS (Souris): I find myself in an unfortunate position, Mr. Speaker. The sponsor of the bill, the bon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson), has been called away on account of sickness in his family. I am a member of the banking and commerce committee, but I was not able to be present when this bill was under consideration due to the unfortunate time at which the meeting was held, and I have not the same intimate knowledge of it. as has my hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer). I desire that this bill be referred back to the committee for a number of reasons. First, I think if the hon. member for Wrest York were present he would be able to make such explanations as would satisfy the house. Secondly, I myself was not present at the meeting of the banking and commerce committee and I should like to hear the discussions which would take place when all persons were present. I am advised that a company known as The Central Finance Corporation is now operating under exactly the same terms as are outlined in this bill, and went through the committee in precisely the same way. I am further advised that the company now in question and the company known as The Central Finance Corporation both operate under the Loan Companies Act and are subject to the inspection of the superintendent of insurance. In themselves these facts are safeguards for the public.

I am not sponsoring the bill, but it does appear to me that when it came before the committee it was the duty of that body to suggest such safeguards as would be beneficial to the general public. It is my further opinion that if through negligence another company has been incorporated which ought not to have been incorporated it is the duty of the committee to take such steps as are necessary with regard to it.

Add this to the $700 interest at seven per cent, and the unhappy borrower is still further behind and gets only $1,260; then he is liable to be charged the same expenses again and again in every case of renewal. And the promoters of the company did not miss anything,-the next subsection provides that in case the company has omitted anything it can charge:

Any officer or. director of the company who does, causes or permits to be done, anything contrary to the provisions of this section shall be liable for each offence to a penalty of not less than twenty dollars and not more than five thousand dollars.
And the other night an hon. member wanted to penalize a farmer not less than $1,000 if he was caught with one per cent more water _ in his butter than the regulations allow! But in this case the wrongdoer is subject to a penalty of not less than $20-in each instance,

No, Mr. Speaker.

No, I have no desire to talk the bill out, and I shall state any observations as rapidly as possible. It does seem to me that two points should be considered with reference to this bill. First, is it of the class which should pass this house at a time when from every part of the country comes the cry of suffering humanity weighed down under a load of debt on which the usual interest charges cannot be paid? By this bill it is proposed to empower another company to charge a still higher rate of interest. I was not a member of the committee, but I have studied the bill with some care, and as far as I can see there is no limitation on the charges of one kind and another that may be made by the company once the borrower has fallen into its clutches. My hon. friend behind me suggests that this might well be
termed a "Shylock" bill-but that the old gentleman is looking for his pound of flesh without giving any undertaking not to shed a drop of blood.
Another point to be considered is this: The bill once having been killed in the select committee, shall it be again referred to that committee? I think we should have finality in these matters. There are only two reasons for a bill being returned to the committee for reconsideration: first, that the bill was not given a fair hearing; no one has suggested that this is so. The other reason is that new evidence may have been forthcoming in the meantime that might change the opinion of the committee; no indication has been given as to that. If the bill has had a hearing before a fair percentage of the committee, is it any more likely at this stage of the session that there will be a full attendance or that the committee will accord the bill a more favourable hearing? In brief, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this bill because of the provisions of the bill itself; I think they are wrong and that they are inopportune. The fact that at another time we gave similar powers to another company is no reason why, in this year of grace, we shoud repeat that error. I am opposed to this bill being returned to the committee, because as far as I can gather the bill has received fair consideration and no new evidence has been brought forward to warrant a re-bearing. The fact that the hon. member who to-day is sponsoring the bill, in the absence of the original sponsor, has not heard the evidence and would desire to hear what is to be said about it is a good argument from his point of view, but that is no reason why it should go back at this time. I hope the house will kill this bill, as it should be killed.

I
just wish to put myself on record as being opposed not only to this particular bill but also to the principle upon which it is based At a time when the majority of the people are criticizing our banks for the rate of interest they are permitted to charge it seems to me it would be a most reactionary thing for this house to pass a bill permitting another company to charge such exorbitant rates of interest. Therefore I am opposed to the principle upon which the bill is based.

It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that these various acts which are general in character have been placed upon the statute books to safe-guard borrowers; I think that may be taken for granted.
