Mr. Chairman, I asked the Minister if he would explain why the item covering stationery and printing shows an amount for 1931-32 of $490,000 as compared with $865,623.18 for 1930-31.

I thank the hon. member
for calling my attention to this matter. The main estimates for 1930-31 called for $490,000 for this item, and this amount was voted during the regime of the former government. However, it was not sufficient to cover the requirements for the year and pay accounts due to the printing bureau which had been accumulating since 1927-28. The present administration decided that these outstanding accounts should be paid, and provided for an amount of $375,623.18 to be included in the supplementary estimates.
The situation to which the hon. member has called attention is one which is likely to arise following any change of government. When main estimates are passed by one administration and further supplementary estimates passed by an incoming administration, it is impossible to avoid this apparent discrepancy in the figures. In order to make a proper comparison it is necessary to show in the figures for the previous year both the main and supplementary estimates which have been passed. I am informed that this has been the practice heretofore. If it were not followed hon. members would find it necessary to have before them the details of the supplementary estimates in order to make a comparison between one year and another. This is not a reflection upon the administration of the former Postmaster General, but is simply the application of a well-defined and long standing rule.

An entirely wrong impression is given by showing in the 1930-31 column the amount of $865,623.18, this being an intimation that the former government had voted that amount. The amount voted by the late administration was $490,000, and if the incoming government found it necessary to straighten out accounts due to the printing department, they should have shown that they were voting $865,623.18 this year instead of $490,000, and then given an explanation of the increase of $375,000. As the two columns now appear an attempt is being made to show that this government is practising economy in that they have reduced one item by $375,000. I do not say that has been done intentionally, but it is a falsification of the records of the former and present government.
The minister says that a precedent has been established for this practice, but I do not know where he gets his information. It has never been the case that an incoming government, having to meet a deficit of an outgoing government, has shown an amount as having been voted by the outgoing government when in fact a part of the amount had been voted by themselves. It is only for that reason that I am pointing this out tonight, that the Post Office Department, under the present government, has not had any decrease; it is not entitled to a decrease of $375,000. What the minister should have had in the estimates was $490,000 plus $375,000, and then showed that the increase he was obliged to make was because of an outstanding account that had not been settled by the former government.

I want to bring to the
minister's attention something that has been referred to me and also I am sure has been referred to him hundreds of times by reason of the many changes in the mail services owing to the cutting off of trains. I have under my hand a communication from the town of Tillsonburg, in the county of Oxford, drawing to my attention the very great handicap under which the industries of that thrifty little town are labouring at the present time. A letter sent to the minister under date of July 14, 1931, explains the position in which many of these towns and villages find themselves, especially those off the main railways that have not at present the mail service
Sup-ply-Post Office

which they enjoyed for many years past-. This is the letter to which I refer:
The Postmaster General,
Parliament Buildings, Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
We are writing you in connection with the change in the postal service in the town of Tillsonburg which came into effect the first of July. Before that date, the mail was delivered here before nine o'clock in the morning, and since then it is ten-thirty, and occasionally if there is any delay such as to-day, it is twelve o'clock noon, and as the last outgoing mail is at two-thirty p.m. you will realize that we have not time to attend to the day's business and it it has _ to stand over for twenty-four hours, which is an intolerable situation for business establishments like ours, and there are a dozen others in this town in the same position.

I would be very glad to hear from you.
Yours very truly,
The Tillsonburg Shoe Company, Limited.
I am sure the minister is conscious of the great handicap under which these industries are labouring. I should like an assurance from him that he will do something and do it soon in order that these towns and villages off the main railroads may receive some consideration.
I should like to bring to his attention another matter which has been referred to me. Many of these mails are carried on mixed trains, part of the train consisting of freight cars, and while they have a schedule on which they are supposed to run, it is very difficult, indeed almost impossible, to run according to schedule, this depending upon the amount of freight they have to lift at the various stations. One can imagine the difficulty with which the postmasters along the route are faced. Some of them tell me they have to wait for these trains an hour, two hours, and so on. Very often it is the wife of the postmaster who has to wait out in those cold stations for the mails to be delivered. I am sure the minister wants to see all of these towns and villages free from this handicap and given the same advantages as industries enjoy in the larger centres which are better served by railways, and that he will do his utmost to see that as soon as at all possible something is done to give these people a fair deal.

I wish to ask him to make amends for what seems to me an injustice committed at St-Lazare, in the county of Bellechasse. The village of St-Lazare, like many of our Quebec villages, is built on both sides of the highway and stretches out lengthwise about a mile. In the centre of the village there is quite a steep hill. For many years the question of where to locate the post office has been debated. It seems that it cannot be located in the centre of the village since the centre is quite a steep hill, the result is that it is located sometimes at one end and at sometimes at the other end. When it is located at the western end, those living in the eastern part complain that it is too far and vice versa. When I was elected as member of Bellechasse, the post office was in the eastern part of the village, close to the church. I was asked to make a change; those living in the western part contended that their end was the business part of the village and they wanted to have the post office there. So as to please everybody, I finally suggested to the Post Office Department to establish two post offices, one at each end of the village, thus endeavouring to get over the difficulty. I was not however successful in my request. After the last election-I must first point out that the postmistress of St-Lazare, until lately, was a Mrs. Leroux-immediately after the elections my opponent in last year's election made a complaint to the Postmaster General, charging Mrs. Leroux with political partizanship. Unfortunately for him he was unable to find any evidence whatsoever in support of his charge. Madame Leroux is an excellent housewife, she minds her own business and does not meddle in politics. Seeing that he could not have her dismissed for political interference, nor obtain an inquiry to that effect, he had recourse to the ever-ready reason that the post office was not in the centre of the village and that it should be placed there. He requested that a person by the name of Adelard Belanger be appointed postmaster to replace Mrs. Leroux. It so happens, however, that Adelard Belanger himself resides quite to the west of the village proper, in the extreme opposite direction to the locality where Mrs. Leroux had the post office. I have letters here which I will not

take up the time of the house in reading, and in which my opponent states to the Postmaster General that it was a question of almost national importance to remove the post office and in the interest of the Conservative party. However, to sum up, the party's interest is that of Adelard Belanger and the , interest of Adelard Belanger is to take away the post office from a mother who is devoted to her family and to have himself appointed postmaster. I have a copy of the Post Office Department's file in this respect before me and I see that all the officials of the Post Office Department from the Deputy Minister down, including the superintendent of the Quebec postal division and inspectors, one after the other wrote to that gentleman, who asked for the dismissal of the postmistress at St. Lazare, that if anything was done, it would be better to settle the question definitely, once for all; because to take the post office from one end to place it at the other, was no solution to the question. Mr. Chairman, on the
question of the dismissal of postmasters and the general changes in the postal service I wish to direct the attention of the committee to a case which I think deserves the very close consideration of the Postmaster General. I wish now to refer to the postmastership of Lakeville, in the county of Carleton, New Brunswick, and in doing so I shall give the history of this post office for as far back as six or seven years at least.
In 1926, when I assumed the office of Postmaster General, a Mr. W. F. Anderson was in charge of the post office at Lakeville. Mr. Anderson was charged, by affidavit, witu political partisanship; an investigation took place, following which he was found guilty of the charge, and on February 21, 1928, an order in council was passed dismissing him. The Civil Service Commission advertised the vacancy and Mr. H. M. Gee was appointed in place of Anderson. Before that appointment was made, in all advertisements it was stated that the applicant must state where he would locate the post office. The applicants did so, and Mr. Gee placed the post office where he said in his application it would be located.
I am informed that Mr. Gee resigned sometime. in May or June, 1930, and the Civil Service Commission, after advertising the vacancy, appointed Mr. S. G. Barter postmaster of Lakeville. In his application Mr. Barter stated that the site would be the same as it had been under the previous postmaster, and Barter was appointed and continued the post office at that point. At the time he asked the Post Office Department, through the superintendent at St. John, New Brunswick, whether he could change the site and the answer was that he could not do so except with the consent of the department. He continued to administer that office in peace and quiet until August.
I have in my hand a certified copy of sessional paper No. 226, containing the correspondence which passed between the present member for Victoria-Carleton and the Post Office Department, together with correspondence between officials of the department and
Mr. Barter, and I wish to place this correspondence on Hansard. Before doing so let me say that Mr. Barter is a returned soldier and the father of six children. Mr. Barter fought overseas for over three years, together with four of his brothers, and he is the only one of those five who has received any consideration from any government or any political party. This is the man who was set aside in order that the post office might be given to a civilian, if the Civil Service Commission would do so. When I was Postmaster General I was accused of not treating returned soldiers as they should have been treated; there was one case in particular, the Simcoe case, into which I will not undertake to go to-night but to which I just refer in passing. If ever a man received a thrashing on the floor of the house; if ever a man was given a calling down, so to speak, I was that man in connection with the Simcoe case, but in that case it could not 'be said that I had discriminated against returned soldiers, because the man who did get the appointment instead of Whittaker was himself a returned man, who in point of qualification was ahead of Whittaker on the list, although under the special sections of the act Whittaker occupied first position because of extreme disability. Here is a case where a man who has done his duty at the front, together with his four brothers, and who has a family of six children, is thrown on the streets. No matter how hard I may have been considered in my treatment of returned soldiers there was never such a case as this brought to my attention.

I have had the case of Lakeville, Carleton county, N.B., about which you wrote on the 29th August, examined.
I find that Mr. W. F. Anderson, who was formerly postmaster at that point, was dismissed by order in council, P.C. 287, of the 21st February, 1928, as guilty of political partisanship. The charges against Mr. Anderson were investigated by a commissioner appointed for the purpose.
I note, however, from your communication, on the dismissal of Mr. Anderson, the office was located on a side street at a point which is very inconvenient so far as the public are concerned, and that the public interest has suffered ever since.	.
The department will have an official report prepared by the district superintendent of postal services, St. John, on the question of the site of the office, on receipt of which your representations on behalf of Miss Hilda Wilson will be given full consideration. I may mention, however, that a permanent appointment in the event of a change will rest with the Civil Service Commission, as the revenue exceeds $400 a year and, therefore, no guarantee can be given that Miss Wilson will be the person selected by the commission for this postmastership.
Yours sincerely,
Arthur Sauve.
The next is a letter from Mr. Underwood to the district superintendent of postal service at St. John, dated September 4, and reading as follows:
The Postmaster General has received representations to the effect that on the dismissal [DOT]of Mr. W. F. Anderson, a former postmaster at Lakeville, N.B., the office was located on a side street running down to the station, which caused great inconvenience to the public. It has been recommended to the Postmaster General that the office be moved to Miss Hilda Wilson's store which is conveniently located and would serve the public well.
Miss Wilson is also stated to be a very competent person.	...
Will District Superintendent please furnish the department with a report on the question of the site of the Lakeville office.
E. J. Underwood.
The next is a letter from the hon. member for Yictoria-Carleton to the Postmaster General, dated September 10, 1930. This letter was written during the special session, and reads as follows:
[Mr. Venict.l
With further reference to my letter of August 29 and your reply of September 4, the recommendation that I made concerning the post office should be carried out. There is no other person there so well qualified and so conveniently located, so far as public service is concerned, to handle this matter as the one I have mentioned, namely, Miss Hilda Wilson.
If that is not a recommendation for a dismissal of a postmaster, I want to know what it is. The letter continues.
I, therefore trust that without undue delay this matter will be given consideration.
Yours very truly,
B. F. Smith.
The next letter dated September 18, 1930, is from the minister to the hon. member, and there is attached a plan of the location. It reads:
I am in receipt of your further letter of the 10th September, asking again that a change be made in the postmastership at Lakeville, N.B.
As you were informed in my previous letter, an official report has been asked for on the question of the site of the office, and, as soon as this report is received, your representations in favour of a change will be dealt with.
The district superintendent of postal service is being asked to make his report on the question as soon as possible.
The next is a letter from Mr. Peck, superintendent of postal service for the St. John district, to the chief superintendent, postal service, Ottawa. It is dated September 16, 1930, and reads as follows:
In reply to the departmental memo, post office, Lakeville, of September 4, requesting that a report be submitted on the question of the present site of the Lakeville post office on the side street where it has been located since the dismissal of Mr. W. F. Anderson, former postmaster, and also stating that it had been recommended to the Postmaster General that the office be moved to a more convenient location at Miss Hilda Wilson's store, the chief superintendent is advised that inspector Allen visited the locality on the 10th instant and reports that the present site of the post office is about 300 yards from the mam highway on a side street leading from the station. It is thus removed from the business and residential part of the community and causes inconvenience.
Miss Hilda Wilson, who is a most competent person, has a store conveniently located in the centre of the village on the main highway and the public could be served much better by the location offered by her. The part of the store that would be used and fitted up for the post office would be commodious and well suited for post office business and the building presents a good appearance.
Enclosed herewith will be found a small sketch showing the locations in question.
The next is a memorandum dated Ottawa, September 30, 1930, which reads:
Memo, for the General Superintendent. Re Lakeville, N.B.

Supply-Post Office
Please allow the question of of this office to stand for the
changing the site present.
L. J. Gaboury, Deputy Postmaster General.
'I he next letter is from the hon. member, dated East Florenceville, N.B., February 24, 1931. It is addressed to Mr. P. T. Coolican' Assistant Deputy Postmaster General. The first part of the letter refers to other matters, but the remainder reads as follows:
I do not believe in making dismissals. I have only asked, I think, for this one-
The hon. member said he did not recommend a dismissal and stated that I could not prove that he had. In this letter he states that he asked only for this one. The letter continues.
-but I have made certain representations in connection with changes notably, the one at Lakeville, New Brunswick, where an injustice was done to the community under the Liberal administration by removing the post office to an inconvenient place for the sake of meeting the wishes of their friends.
It was not made to meet the wishes of our friends, because the appointment was made under civil service regulations, and the site was described in the application. The letter continues:
I asked to have this office moved back to where it would be convenient for the public. My information is, that the superintendent at fct. John was asked to make a report upon it and while in St. John recently, I gathered that has report recommended the change which I had made, however, the .matter stands and nothing has been done.
I am too busy with business matters to spend my time in writing a number of letters about these matters and when I make a recommendation I think I know the ground that I am working upon. Until some action has been taken by your department to carry out recommendations already made along this line, I shall not be in a position to waste further time in trying to give advice.
Yours truly,
B. F. Smith.
The next is a letter from Mr. Coolican to the hon. member at East Florenceville. It is dated February 27, 1931, and reads:
J duly received your communication of the 24th instant, respecting Benton and Lakeville post offices.
I have noted your remarks and I may say that if you will call at my office as soon as you arrive in Ottawa, I shall be pleased to go into these questions further with you.
If the hon. member was in the same mood when he called on Mr. Coolican as he was when he wrote his previous letter, I pity Mr. Coolican. The next is a memorandum signed by Mr. Gaboury to the general superintendent. It is dated March 31, 1931. and reads:
Lakeville, New Brunswick.
The Postmaster General has authorized the removal of the office to the main road where it was located some years ago.
Please place office in temporary charge Miss i 'Vllson, pending a permanent appointment by the commission.
What authority had the Postmaster General or even the governor in council to dismiss Mr. Barter and place the office in charge of this young lady ? Under the regulations of the Civil Service Act a dismissal can be made in two or perhaps three ways. First, if the postmaster in the administration of his office is not giving satisfaction and the district superintendent so reports, then the minister, under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, has authority to act. Second, if the postmaster is guilty of political partisanship and a charge is made against him under an affidavit by some reliable person, the minister may order an investigation, and if it results in proving the political charges against the postmaster, the latter may be dismissed by ol der in council. Third, if the postmaster is guilty or suspected of being guilty of political partisanship and the sitting member for the constituency gives a certificate that the man has been guilty of political partisanship, then he may be dismissed by order in council. There is no other way under the sun of dismissing a postmaster.

Can
he not be dismissed for the good of the service?
Not under the Civil Service Commission.

Did
the hon. member not do so?
Mr. VEhilOT: I did not. The hon. member cannot point to a Civil Service Commission case where I dismissed a postmaster without first, if the charge was one of maladministration, an investigation by the departmental officials; second, if the charge was one of political partisanship, without an investigation; or, third, if the charge was political partisanship, without the recommendation of the sitting member that he had personal knowledge of the matter.

With
all due deference to my hon. friend-
I do not care what deference my hon. friend may have, he cannot point to a case.

The
hon. member had some twenty-seven dismissals in the county of Victoria-Carletoa
Supply-Post Office

which were on the recommendation of Michael Dwyer, who was not the sitting member.

Those are dismissals of
postmasters where the revenue is under $400 per annum, who therefore do not come under the Civil Service Commission.

But
the hon. member dismissed them just the same.

I am directed by the Postmaster General to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 18th instant respecting the change in the postmastership at Lakeville.
As the postmaster was notified a few days ago, the change at that point was authorized in order to place the office in a more central location.
It may be added, however, that the permanent appointment rests with the Civil Service Commission and that the vacancy will, therefore, have to be advertised publicly in Lakeville in the near future and the case referred to the Civil Service Commission.
Yours very truly,
L. J. Gaboury,
Deputy Postmaster General.
I go on.
Oh, oh.

Yes, there are quite a few letters yet, but this is nothing compared with over 150 pages of Hansard in 1929 that were taken up by the present Prime Minister reading into the record the files of my department. If he thought fit at that time, owing to the administration of the Post Office Department, to take up the time of the house and fill 160 pages of Hansard, surely I am entitled to take up a little time to put this case on record.
That was nice cool weather.

And that had reference to
only one case, and it took him over five hours to put it on record.

He had a good case.
Supply-Post Office

It was a good case, but
it did him no good, and it did me no harm.
Here is a copy of a letter to the Postmaster General from Mr. Barter, in which he says: Letter received re dismissal as postmaster. No notice of the wish of the department to change site of post office was ever received. This is only an excuse. Had bought post office and notified superintendent at St. John that soon as I obtained a proper site I would ask his approval. Could not move office without permission. Miss Wilson, to whom the office is to be given, is the daughter of one of our late leading merchants, and she has a large country village store.
Had I received order to move post office I would have done so, but the very people who were complaining would not give or sell me land to put the building on. I most eagerly ask for a hearing before the postmastershdp is taken from me.
Miss Wilson has only to maintain a widowed mother, and she runs the country store in Lakeville. Relying upon Hilda Wilson I find that the estate is given a credit of about 810,000. If it is necessary to throw out of office a returned soldier with a family of six or seven children to help a young lady keep her widowed mother, who owns a large estate which is rated at 810,000, then I think it is time that some change should be made in the method of dealing with these matters.
I have a letter here from H. B. Peck, which I will pass over.
We shall not miss anything.
Perhaps you will find before I get through that I have not missed anything.

Tell us something about
how the man who was dismissed was appointed.

He was appointed by the
Civil Service Commission in the month of June, 1930, after examination.

It was
before that.

Then the record must be
wrong, for it shows that Barter was appointed in June, 1930. I did not even know that Barter was appointed, because from June 3, 1930, until after the federal elections were over I did not visit Ottawa. So far as that was concerned I did not know what was going on because this was a matter of departmental administration which could be carried on without my knowledge.
Mr, SMITH (Victoria-Carleton): The office was transferred before.

My hon. friend is not stating the facts. In 1928 Gee was appointed. Gee had a crippled son whom he had sworn in 
to carry on the office work, but the crippled son could not carry on the full work of the office and Mr. Barter was engaged as a second assistant by Gee to come at different periods to do the work of the office in conjunction with Mr. Gee's son. When Mr. Gee retired, owing to the fact that his son could no longer look after anything he resigned and a vacancy was advertised. Barter applied for the position and under Civil Service qualifications he got the appointment. That is the record of the transaction, and the documents show that my statements are in accordance with the facts. My hon. friends opposite need not try to speak contrary to the record.
Now then, there are a number of other letters in the file. Mr. MeBurney again protests, and we have a letter signed by Mr. Peck relating to the change. Then we have the particulars to be furnished upon appointments of postmasters and revenue officers in connection with which a blank form is supplied. I am endeavouring to point out the whole record. Then follows a letter from H. B. Peck, of St. John, in which he says:
With reference to departmental memorandum, 38/77, of the 2nd instant, advising of the dismissal of S. G. Barter, postmaster at the above address, and instructing that the office be placed in the temporary charge of Miss Hilda Wilson, the chief superintendent is informed that the office was duly transferred to the charge of the incoming acting postmistress on the 22nd instant.
I do not want to state that the information given by Mr. Peck is not correct; technically it is correct. Mr. Peck went there to make a transfer, and it was understood the transfer would take place. However when Mr. Barter undertook to hand over the position to Miss Wilson she could not accept it because she had not her store prepared to accept the transfer of the office, and she asked Mr. Barter to continue for another week. Mr. Barter was foolish enough to do so. Had I been in his place I would Shave thrown the stuff out on the street; that is what I would have done. Miss Wilson would not take charge of it; she was appointed to take charge of it, but when the time came she could not take over the work.
That is all I have to say in connection with this particular case, and as it is-
Eleven o'clock.

-about eleven o'clodk. I shall not continue further to-night. If hon. members wish I shall continue right up to the minute, but I should prefer to go on at a later time. I have more cases than the present one in connection with which I intend to make some statements-hon. members need not make any mistake about that. I have

Railways and Shipping Report
taken too much from my hon. friends opposite to let things slip. They have condemned me for acts of which they themselves are guilty. They attempted to crucify me for things they are now doing.
Shame.

Some of the older members in the house who hear my voice will remember their actions during the session of 1929. I am not blaming the Postmaster General in matters of this kind. He is a new man, unacquainted with the intricacies of his office. I know that I found it difficult to learn the ropes in that department. However, I had had the experience of administering another department which stood me in good stead when I came to the larger department; my friend however did not have that experience. I am not blaming him, but I blame his colleagues who sat in council with him when these matters were considered-the same gentlemen who sat day in and day out on this side of the house and refused to allow my estimates to go through, criticizing me about matters far less important than the one we have just considered. His colleagues must have known that a dismissal of a civil servant brought about in the manner I have described was illegal, and they should have drawn the fact to the attention of their colleague who had recently taken office and did not know the ins and outs of the Civil Service Act.
Progress reported.
